messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Priya

Priya was sixty-six years old when she came to the clinic, though her posture and the careful way she moved suggested someone older, someone who had learned to take up less space. She had been working in retail for thirty-eight years, a steady job that had sustained her through her marriage to Rajesh and, after his death five years ago, had kept her anchored to routine and purpose. That anchor had come loose two years before she sought help.

The assault happened on a March evening in 2021, in the storage room behind the clothing store where she worked. A man came in as she was closing—someone she did not recognize, someone who had drifted past the registers and slipped through the back door while she was restocking. He was younger than her, with a smell like stale cigarettes and something chemical, and he moved with the kind of deliberate slowness that told her immediately what was about to happen. The attack lasted perhaps ten minutes, though Priya could never say for certain. What remained were not minutes but moments: his hand over her mouth, the concrete wall against her back, the particular angle of the fluorescent light above her head, the smell—that smell—which had seemed to coat everything, including her skin. She had not reported it to police. She had not told anyone for six months. When she finally told her daughter, Priya had felt something shift in the family's regard for her, as though she had become a different kind of person, someone marked. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. The job that had defined her, the routines that had steadied her, the sense that she had built something—all of it had collapsed into a kind of gray meaninglessness.

The first few months after the assault, Priya had tried to return to work. But the storage room had become impossible. More than that, the store itself had become a place where her body would not cooperate. A customer would enter who was male, someone she did not know, and her heart would begin to race. She found herself unable to be alone with any man—a coworker, a customer, even the owner—without her chest tightening, without the urge to move away becoming overwhelming. Being alone with men had become a trigger that pulled her back into the storage room, and when she was pulled back, the memories came with a clarity that was almost photographic. She could see the light fixture. She could see the exact expression on his face. She could see the position of his hands. The memories did not feel like memories; they felt like looking at photographs, vivid and unchanging, except that some of them were missing entirely. There were blank spaces in the sequence—gaps where her mind had simply refused to record what was happening—and those blanks were somehow worse than the clarity, because they left her with the feeling that she did not even have the full story of what had been done to her.

After three months of not being able to work, Priya had stopped going in. She told her manager she was ill. She told her daughter she needed time. What she meant was that she could not bear the unpredictability of who might walk through the door, the constant vigilance required to know whether she would be alone with a man, the way that particular kind of fear would trigger the memories again and again—the photographs in her mind playing in sequence, the smell returning even though she was safe, the feeling of unfairness rising in her chest like something that would choke her. What happened to her was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. No one had been caught. No one had been held accountable. And every time a man approached her, every time she caught the smell of smoke or fire on someone's clothes, every time she witnessed someone behaving in a way that felt like a violation of decency—someone being rude to a cashier, someone cutting in line, someone speaking harshly—the memories would flood back, and with them came the certainty that she could not deal with even the slightest upset. The smallest frustration would send her into a state of near-collapse. She had become, in her own mind, someone fragile and broken, someone who had lost the capacity to manage ordinary life.

She came to the clinic because her daughter had insisted, because the isolation had become complete, because she had begun to wonder if there was any point in continuing at all. What she wanted most was to feel that her life still meant something. What she feared most was that it never would again.
